title: Causes and Explanations: A Structural-Model Approach, Part I: Causes
authors: Joseph Y. Halpern, Judea Pearl
venue: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science (arXiv cs/0011012)
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural causal models (structural equations, causal settings (M,u))
formal_object: When a conjunction of primitive events X=x is an actual (token) cause of an event phi in a causal setting: but-for dependence under a contingency W=w', a sufficiency clause, and minimality.
key_formula: AC1: (M,\vec u)\models(\vec X=\vec x)\wedge\varphi.\ AC2: \exists (\vec Z,\vec W),\ \vec X\subseteq\vec Z,\ (\vec x',\vec w'):\ (a)\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w']\neg\varphi;\ (b)\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x,\vec W'\leftarrow\vec w',\vec Z'\leftarrow\vec z^*]\varphi\ \forall\vec W'\subseteq\vec W,\vec Z'\subseteq\vec Z.\ AC3: \vec X\ \text{minimal}. (updated definition, as restated in the appendix of Part II)
assumptions: A known, fully specified (recursive) causal model with chosen endogenous/exogenous variables and a known context; verdicts are model-relative.
relevance: The base definition the user plans to build on: a faithful CoT could be one whose stated reasons are actual causes of the answer; AC2's contingencies handle redundant/backup reasoning paths that defeat plain but-for (deletion) tests.

title: Causes and Explanations: A Structural-Model Approach. Part II: Explanations
authors: Joseph Y. Halpern, Judea Pearl
venue: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science (conference version IJCAI 2001; arXiv cs/0208034)
formalism: structural causal models + epistemic state (set K of contexts, optionally a probability)
formal_object: An explanation of phi relative to the contexts K an agent considers possible: a minimal X=x that is a sufficient cause of phi wherever it holds in K and is not already known; plus partial explanations and explanatory power.
key_formula: EX1: (M,\vec u)\models\varphi\ \forall\vec u\in\mathcal K;\ EX2: \vec X=\vec x\ \text{is a sufficient cause of}\ \varphi\ \text{in}\ (M,\vec u)\ \forall\vec u\in\mathcal K\ \text{with}\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec X=\vec x;\ EX3: \vec X\ \text{minimal};\ EX4: (M,\vec u)\models\neg(\vec X=\vec x)\ \text{for some}\ \vec u\in\mathcal K\ \text{and}\ (M,\vec u')\models\vec X=\vec x\ \text{for some}\ \vec u'\in\mathcal K
assumptions: Known causal model (or a set of candidate models in the general version), an explicit epistemic state K of the explainee, a prior Pr for partial explanations.
relevance: Gives a formal notion of explanation that is relative to the explainee's knowledge; this suggests separating faithfulness (explanation w.r.t. the LLM's true model) from plausibility (explanation w.r.t. the reader's model). Sufficiency is a candidate formalization of completeness.

title: Actual Causality
authors: Joseph Y. Halpern
formalism: structural causal models, normality orderings, probability over causal settings
formal_object: Three variants of HP actual causation (original, updated, modified), graded causation via normality, degree of responsibility and blame, explanation as sufficient cause relative to an epistemic state, partial explanations with goodness (alpha,beta) and explanatory power.
key_formula: \text{Explanatory power (Def. 7.2.5)}:\ \Pr(\mathcal K(\vec X=\vec x,\varphi,\mathrm{SC2})\mid[\![\vec X=\vec x]\!]);\quad db(\mathcal K,\Pr,X=x,\varphi)=\sum_{(M,\vec u)\in\mathcal K}dr((M,\vec u),X=x,\varphi)\Pr((M,\vec u))
assumptions: Known causal model or a probability over causal settings; choice of variables matters (model relativity, Ch. 4); normality ordering if graded causation is used.
relevance: The reference for every definition the user needs: the modified HP definition (lowest complexity), graded responsibility and blame, explanatory power, and the book's own treatment of how to choose variables, which an LLM application must justify. Local copy in actual-causality/.

title: Responsibility and blame: a structural-model approach
authors: Hana Chockler, Joseph Y. Halpern
formalism: structural causal models + epistemic state (probability over causal settings)
formal_object: Degree of responsibility of X=x for phi: 1/(k+1), with k the minimal number of variables that must change to make phi counterfactually depend on X=x; degree of blame: expected responsibility over an agent's epistemic state.
key_formula: dr((M,\vec u),(X=x),\varphi)=0\ \text{if}\ X=x\ \text{is not a cause of}\ \varphi;\ \text{else}\ \tfrac{1}{k+1},\ k=\min\#\{W\in\vec W:\ w'_W\neq W(\vec u)\}\ \text{over witnesses}\ ((\vec Z,\vec W),(x',\vec w'))\ \text{satisfying AC2}
assumptions: Known causal model and context for responsibility; a probability over causal settings (the agent's epistemic state) for blame.
relevance: The standard graded notion: could grade how much each CoT step or verbalized factor is responsible for the answer, and blame could separate what a model 'could have known' (relevant to intent and sandbagging arguments).

title: A Modification of the Halpern-Pearl Definition of Causality
authors: Joseph Y. Halpern
formalism: structural causal models
formal_object: Modified HP definition: contingency variables W are frozen at their actual values; simpler, handles Hopkins-Pearl problems, lower complexity (D_1^P) than the original and updated definitions.
key_formula: AC2(a^m):\ \exists\vec W\subseteq\mathcal V\setminus\vec X,\ \vec w^*,\ \vec x':\ (M,\vec u)\models\vec W=\vec w^*\ \wedge\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x',\vec W\leftarrow\vec w^*]\neg\varphi\ \text{(as restated in Halpern and Pass 2025, Def. 2.1)}
assumptions: Known causal model and context.
relevance: The variant Halpern currently prefers; freezing contingencies at actual values maps naturally onto 'hold the rest of the CoT/activations as they were' interventions.

title: Causality Without Causal Models
authors: Joseph Y. Halpern, Rafael Pass
formalism: abstract counterfactual structures (Lewis/Stalnaker-style), modal logic of counterfactuals
formal_object: An abstract HP-style definition of actual cause (and of explanation) for any model with counterfactuals; causes and effects may be arbitrary formulas, including disjunctions, negations, beliefs and nested counterfactuals; allows backtracking.
key_formula: AC1': (M,s)\models\varphi\wedge\psi;\ AC2': \exists\tau\in\mathcal C_X:\ (M,s)\models\tau\ \text{and}\ (M,s)\models(\neg\varphi\wedge\tau)\rightarrow\neg\psi;\ AC3': \varphi\ \text{minimal}
assumptions: A counterfactual structure (closeness/selection function) and a chosen set C_X of allowable contingency formulas; no structural equations needed.
relevance: Removes the need for an explicit SCM over CoT tokens and allows causes that are beliefs or formulas, which a definition of 'the stated reason caused the answer' or of self-report accuracy needs.

title: Causal Explanations and XAI
authors: Sander Beckers
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural causal models
formal_object: Weak, direct and strong sufficiency; sufficient explanations (X=x,N) with a safeguarded network N; counterfactual explanations as contrastive analogs; actual causation defined from good sufficient explanations.
key_formula: (\vec X=\vec x,\vec N)\ \text{is a sufficient explanation of}\ Y=y\ \text{iff}\ \vec X=\vec x\ \text{is strongly sufficient for}\ Y=y\ \text{along}\ \vec N:\ Y\in\vec N\ \wedge\ \forall\vec c\in R(\vec C),\vec u:\ (M,\vec u)\models[\vec X\leftarrow\vec x,\vec C\leftarrow\vec c]\vec N=\vec n,\ \vec C=\mathcal V-(\vec X\cup\vec N)
assumptions: Known causal model of the inputs and the ML model's output; the explanation must name which variables are safeguarded from interventions.
relevance: Formal account of when an explanation of an ML output is correct and action-guiding; distinguishes kinds of sufficiency that matter for whether a CoT's reasons 'suffice' for the answer (completeness) and gives counterfactual explanations a causal semantics.

title: Large Language Models as Nondeterministic Causal Models
authors: Sander Beckers
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: nondeterministic causal models
formal_object: A semantics for counterfactuals of probabilistic LLMs by representing an LLM as a nondeterministic causal model; contrasts it with the Gumbel-max deterministic SCM representation of Chatzi et al. and Ravfogel et al.
assumptions: Black-box access to the LLM's conditional output distribution; no implementation details needed.
relevance: Supplies the missing step for applying HP to LLMs: a principled causal model of the LLM itself, so that 'had the CoT/prompt been different, the answer would have been...' is well defined.

title: Causal Sufficiency and Necessity Improves Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
authors: Xiangning Yu, Zhuohan Wang, Linyi Yang, Haoxuan Li, Anjie Liu, Xiao Xue, Jun Wang, Mengyue Yang
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: probabilities of causation (Pearl) over an SCM of CoT steps
formal_object: Probability of sufficiency of a reasoning chain and probability of necessity / PNS of an individual CoT step for the correct answer, with identifiability results; used to prune or add steps.
key_formula: PN(S,s_t,q)=P\big(A_{do(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t})}\neq y\mid A=y,S,q\big);\quad PNS(S,s_t,q):=P(A_S=y,\ A_{S'}\neq y),\ S'=(s_{<t},\bar s_t,s'_{>t})
assumptions: Answer is a function of the CoT; interventions replace a step with a corrupted variant and regenerate later steps; correct answer known.
relevance: The only work found that applies counterfactual necessity/sufficiency to CoT steps; targets correctness and efficiency rather than faithfulness, and uses Pearl's PN/PS, not HP actual causation (no contingencies).

title: Explaining Image Classifiers
authors: Hana Chockler, Joseph Y. Halpern
formalism: structural causal models (Halpern 2016 explanation)
formal_object: Halpern's explanation (necessity and sufficiency clauses, restriction of options considered) applied to a classifier's output; shows Mothilal et al. use a stronger condition; covers explanations of absence and of rare events.
assumptions: The classifier is the causal model; input features (pixels/regions) are the variables; a set of contexts the agent considers.
relevance: Shows how to instantiate HP explanation for a learned model's output and where popular XAI definitions deviate from it; a template for defining what a correct explanation of an LLM answer is.

title: Causal Explanations for Image Classifiers
authors: Hana Chockler, David A. Kelly, Daniel Kroening, Youcheng Sun
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, vol. 86, 2026
formalism: actual causality and causal responsibility
formal_object: Black-box explanations of image classifier outputs grounded in actual causality; approximate explanations with proven termination, complexity and approximation bounds (tool ReX).
assumptions: Black-box query access; a masking/occlusion baseline defines interventions.
relevance: The main working implementation of HP explanation plus responsibility ranking for neural models; shows how to approximate the definition at scale.

title: Sufficient, Necessary and Complete Causal Explanations in Image Classification
authors: David A. Kelly, Hana Chockler
formalism: actual causality; logic-based (abductive) explanations
formal_object: Sufficient and necessary causal explanations, their equivalence to logic-based explanations, and delta-complete / 1-complete explanations (explanation classified with at least a given confidence).
assumptions: Black-box access; classifier confidence available.
relevance: Gives formal causal notions of sufficiency, necessity and completeness of an explanation, which map onto the completeness and soundness requirements in the user's scope.

title: Probabilities of Causation: Bounds and Identification
authors: Jin Tian, Judea Pearl
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural counterfactuals / potential outcomes
formal_object: Probability of necessity (PN), sufficiency (PS) and both (PNS) of a binary cause for a binary effect, with sharp bounds from experimental and observational data.
key_formula: PN=P(Y_{x'}=\text{false}\mid X=\text{true},Y=\text{true})=P(y'_{x'}\mid x,y);\quad PS=P(y_x\mid y',x')
assumptions: Binary variables (extensions possible); a structural model; identification needs exogeneity/monotonicity or bounds.
relevance: The probabilistic counterpart of but-for causation used by every PN/PS-based CoT and rationale paper; a population-level alternative when HP's token-level setting is too fine for stochastic LLMs.

title: Local Explanations via Necessity and Sufficiency: Unifying Theory and Practice
authors: David Watson, Limor Gultchin, Ankur Taly, Luciano Floridi
formalism: probability over a context distribution; logic of factors; causal interventions optional
formal_object: A basis (f, D, C, ordering); probability that a factor is sufficient / necessary for an output; tau-minimal sufficient factors; unifies SHAP, anchors and counterfactuals; sound and complete algorithm LENS.
key_formula: PS(c,y):=P(f(z)=y\mid c(z)=1);\quad PN(c,y):=P(c(z)=1\mid f(z)=y),\ z\sim\mathcal D
assumptions: A target function, a context distribution D (observational or interventional), a set of candidate factors.
relevance: Shows that common XAI explanations are necessity/sufficiency claims relative to a context distribution; the choice of D is exactly the choice of counterfactual inputs in CoT faithfulness tests.

title: Contrastive Explanation: A Structural-Model Approach
authors: Tim Miller
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural causal models (extends Halpern 2015)
formal_object: Contrastive counterfactual cause and contrastive bi-factual cause: answers to 'why phi rather than psi' as pairs of partial causes differing minimally.
key_formula: \langle\vec X=\vec x,\vec X=\vec y\rangle:\ CC1\ \vec X=\vec x\ \text{partial cause of}\ \varphi\ \text{in}\ (M,\vec u);\ CC2\ (M,\vec u)\models\neg\psi;\ CC3\ \exists\vec W,\vec w:\ \vec X=\vec y\ \text{partial cause of}\ \psi\ \text{in}\ (M_{\vec W\leftarrow\vec w},\vec u);\ CC4\ (\vec X=\vec x)\cap(\vec X=\vec y)=\emptyset;\ CC5\ \vec X\ \text{maximal}
assumptions: Known causal model; an explicit foil psi.
relevance: Formalizes the contrastive questions behind counterfactual faithfulness tests (why answer A rather than B) within HP; the formal follow-up of Miller's 2019 survey.

title: Towards Formal Definitions of Blameworthiness, Intention, and Moral Responsibility
authors: Joseph Y. Halpern, Max Kleiman-Weiner
formalism: structural causal models + epistemic state (probability over causal models) + utility
formal_object: Degree of blameworthiness and intention relative to an epistemic state (a probability over causal models and a utility on outcomes); combined with actual causality to give moral responsibility.
assumptions: The agent's probability over causal models and utility function must be specified or inferred.
relevance: An HP-based formal definition of intention, relevant to scheming, covert goals and sandbagging; links intent to actual causation, which a causal account of hidden objectives could reuse.

title: Actual Causation and Nondeterministic Causal Models
authors: Sander Beckers
formalism: nondeterministic causal models
formal_object: A definition of actual causation in nondeterministic causal models, built from generalized counterfactual dependence and structural simplification; verdicts close to Beckers 2021/2022.
assumptions: A nondeterministic causal model; applies to deterministic models as a special case.
relevance: Actual causation for stochastic mechanisms, which sampled LLM reasoning is; pairs with Beckers' LLMs-as-nondeterministic-models paper as a route to HP-style token causation for CoT.

title: Gumbel Counterfactual Generation From Language Models
authors: Shauli Ravfogel, Anej Svete, Vésteinn Snæbjarnarson, Ryan Cotterell
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural equation model via the Gumbel-max trick
formal_object: Reformulates an LM as a structural equation model with Gumbel sampling noise, giving a joint distribution over an observed string and its counterfactual under an intervention; hindsight Gumbel sampling infers the noise.
assumptions: Access to next-token logits; the Gumbel-max representation of sampling (contested by Beckers 2025).
relevance: Makes rung-3 counterfactuals of LLM generations computable, so HP-style conditions ('holding the sampling noise fixed, had step t differed') can be evaluated on real CoTs.

title: Towards Trustworthy Explanation: On Causal Rationalization
authors: Wenbo Zhang, Tong Wu, Yunlong Wang, Yong Cai, Hengrui Cai
formalism: structural causal model of rationalization; probabilities of causation
formal_object: A structural causal model of rationale selection and probabilities of causation (necessity and sufficiency) of text snippets, with identification, used to learn non-spurious, efficient rationales.
assumptions: Proposed SCM of rationalization; identification conditions; extractive rationales of text classifiers.
relevance: The closest NLP use of causal necessity/sufficiency to define a correct (non-spurious) rationale; extractive rather than generated, so it does not cover verbalized CoT.

title: Explaining Black-Box Algorithms Using Probabilistic Contrastive Counterfactuals
authors: Sainyam Galhotra, Romila Pradhan, Babak Salimi
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: probabilistic contrastive counterfactuals (probabilities of causation) over a causal diagram
formal_object: Necessity, sufficiency and necessity-and-sufficiency scores of attribute values for a black-box decision, at local, contextual and global levels, plus recourse (system LEWIS).
assumptions: A causal diagram over inputs (or background knowledge), identification of counterfactual probabilities.
relevance: Replaces associational 'responsibility' scores in XAI with probabilities of causation; a population-level graded alternative to Chockler-Halpern responsibility.

title: Explanation in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Social Sciences
authors: Tim Miller
formalism: none (semi-formal survey of philosophy and psychology)
formal_object: Semi-formal: explanations are contrastive, selected, social, and causal rather than statistical. Formal definitions build on it, notably Miller 2021 (contrastive explanation in SCMs).
relevance: Influential semi-formal framework recorded because formal contrastive definitions build on it; useful for separating what humans find explanatory (plausibility) from what is causally correct.

title: Does Reasoning Emerge? Examining the Probabilities of Causation in Large Language Models
authors: Javier González, Aditya V. Nori
formalism: probabilities of causation (PN, PS)
formal_object: Conditions under which an LLM's approximations of PN and PS for a reasoning problem can be computed and compared to the true mechanism, as a test of whether LLMs reason.
assumptions: A known ground-truth causal mechanism (math problems); LLM treated as an abstract machine with a natural-language interface.
relevance: Applies PN/PS to LLMs, but to the correctness of reasoning about a world model, not to whether stated reasoning causes the output.

title: Slaying the Hydra: Interaction-Aware Circuit Discovery in Language Models
authors: Sankaran Vaidyanathan, Rafal Urbaniak, Emily Bunnapradist, Michelangelo Naim, Daniel Waxman
formalism: actual causality (witnesses) with expectations over cause and witness sets
formal_object: Witness-integrated set effect (WISE), causal estimands that average HP-style witness contingencies over sets of components, used to rank LM components for circuit discovery.
assumptions: White-box access to model components; interventions on activations.
relevance: Brings HP witnesses (contingencies) to LLM internals, addressing backup components that defeat one-at-a-time ablation; the same issue arises for redundant CoT steps.

title: Honesty Is the Best Policy: Defining and Mitigating AI Deception
authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Francesco Belardinelli, Francesca Toni, Tom Everitt
formalism: structural causal games (SCGs)
formal_object: Belief as acceptance (agent acts as if it observed phi true, for phi it responds to); intentionally causing outcomes; deception = S intentionally causes T's decision, T believes false phi, S does not believe phi; sound and complete graphical criteria.
key_formula: Belief (Def. 3.1): D^i(\pi,e)=D^i_{\phi=\top}(\pi_{i(\phi)},e). Intention (Def. 3.4): \sum_{U\in\mathcal U^i}\mathbb E_{\pi}[U]\le\sum_{U\in\mathcal U^i}\mathbb E_{(\hat\pi^i,\pi^{-i})}[U_{\{Y_{\pi|w_Y}\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}}] with subset-minimal \mathbf Y\supseteq\mathbf X, w_Y. Deception (Def. 3.7): 1) S intentionally causes D^T=D^T(\pi,e); 2) T believes \phi and \phi is false; 3) S does not believe \phi.
assumptions: Agents share a correct SCG; belief identifiable only when the agent responds to phi; phi not a descendant of the decision; a reference set of alternative policies; LMs treated as agents whose policy adapts to prompt interventions.
relevance: Most complete concept-level formalisation in the area. Theorem 3.6: intention implies HP actual causation. Its belief test (insert phi into the prompt, check whether behaviour changes) has the same form as cue-injection CoT faithfulness tests.

title: The Reasons that Agents Act: Intention and Instrumental Goals
authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Matt MacDermott, Francesco Belardinelli, Francesca Toni, Tom Everitt
formalism: structural causal influence models (SCIMs), policy oracles
formal_object: Subjective intention relative to the agent's SCIM and utility (Def. 6); behavioural intention of a policy oracle: fixing the intended outcomes by contextual intervention changes the chosen policy (Def. 13); the two are equivalent under robust optimality (Thm. 14).
key_formula: Def. 6: \mathbb E_{\pi}[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U]\le\mathbb E_{\hat\pi}[\sum_{U\in\mathbf U}U_{\mathbf Y_{\pi}|\mathbf W}], \mathbf W=\{w_Y\}_{Y\in\mathbf Y}, \mathbf Y and every w_Y subset-minimal. Def. 13: \Gamma(\mathcal M)\neq\Gamma(\mathcal M_{\mathbf Y_{\pi}|\mathbf W}).
assumptions: Observer and agent share a causal model of the environment; reference policy set; behavioural version needs only interventional access to the policy, and equivalence to subjective intent needs a robustly optimal oracle.
relevance: Behavioural intention needs no access to utilities, only input interventions, so it can test whether an LLM acts for the reason its CoT states; relates intent to actual causality and instrumental control incentives.

title: Reasoning about Causality in Games
authors: Lewis Hammond, James Fox, Tom Everitt, Ryan Carey, Alessandro Abate, Michael Wooldridge
concepts: framework for belief, intention and deception
formalism: (structural) causal games: Pearl's causal hierarchy extended to multi-agent influence diagrams
formal_object: Causal games at the associational, interventional and counterfactual levels; uniform modelling of dependencies between variables and between strategies; how causal queries are computed in games and under which assumptions.
assumptions: Decisions modelled as variables with policies; rationality or equilibrium assumptions to answer interventional and counterfactual queries on policies.
relevance: The substrate of Ward's definitions; extends SCMs (hence HP) to settings with a model, an overseer and a monitor, so one framework could host deception, monitorability and faithfulness.

title: Agent Incentives: A Causal Perspective
authors: Tom Everitt, Ryan Carey, Eric Langlois, Pedro A. Ortega, Shane Legg
formalism: causal influence diagrams
formal_object: Value of information, value of control, response incentives and instrumental control incentives (whether an agent can influence its utility via X), each with sound and complete graphical criteria.
assumptions: Known causal influence diagram; optimal policies.
relevance: Incentive concepts behind Ward's graphical criteria for deception; an instrumental control incentive on an overseer's or monitor's belief is a natural formal precursor of scheming or obfuscation incentives.

title: Discovering Agents
authors: Zachary Kenton, Ramana Kumar, Sebastian Farquhar, Jonathan Richens, Matt MacDermott, Tom Everitt
formalism: causal models, mechanised causal graphs, game-theoretic influence diagrams
formal_object: Agents as systems that would adapt their policy if their actions influenced the world differently; a causal discovery algorithm for agents; translation between causal models and influence diagrams.
assumptions: Interventional access to the system's mechanisms; a causal model of the system.
relevance: Provides the adaptivity criterion behind Ward's behavioural belief and intention; needed to justify treating an LLM as an agent to which beliefs and intentions can be ascribed.

title: Measuring Goal-Directedness
authors: Matt MacDermott, James Fox, Francesco Belardinelli, Tom Everitt
formalism: maximum causal entropy in causal models and MDPs
formal_object: Maximum entropy goal-directedness (MEG): how well a policy is predicted by maximum-causal-entropy optimisation of a known utility, a hypothesis class of utilities, or a set of variables; algorithms and desiderata.
assumptions: A causal model or MDP; a utility function or hypothesis class.
relevance: The only formal account found of an agent pursuing a goal; could ground the 'pursues an objective' clause in definitions of hidden objectives and scheming.

title: Truthful AI: Developing and governing AI that does not lie
authors: Owain Evans, Owen Cotton-Barratt, Lukas Finnveden, Adam Bales, Avital Balwit, Peter Wills, Luca Righetti, William Saunders
formalism: first-order logical schema (semi-formal) plus governance norms
formal_object: Truthful, Honest and Undeluded as universally quantified implications over statements and beliefs; an AI lie is a false statement strongly strategically selected and optimised for the speaker's benefit; a standard of avoiding negligent falsehoods.
key_formula: \mathrm{Truthful}:=\forall S\,(\mathrm{states}(S)\Rightarrow\mathrm{is\_true}(S));\ \mathrm{Undeluded}:=\forall S\,(\mathrm{believes}(S)\Rightarrow\mathrm{is\_true}(S));\ \mathrm{Honest}:=\forall S\,(\mathrm{states}(S)\Rightarrow\mathrm{believes}(S))
assumptions: A belief predicate for the AI, left undefined; a notion of statement; degrees of each property are left informal.
relevance: The standard honest-versus-truthful split; semi-formal, and Ward et al. build on it. It becomes a formal definition once 'believes' is given by an SCG belief; an honest CoT would state only believed steps.

title: Standards for Belief Representations in LLMs
authors: Daniel A. Herrmann, Benjamin A. Levinstein
formalism: adequacy conditions drawn from decision theory and formal epistemology
formal_object: Four adequacy criteria for an internal LLM representation to count as belief-like: accuracy, coherence, uniformity and use.
assumptions: Access to internal representations; criteria are conditions, not a mathematical definition.
relevance: The main philosophical account of what an LLM belief must satisfy; complements Ward's behavioural acceptance with conditions on internal representations, which a definition of lying (stated content differs from belief) needs.

title: Defining Deception in Decision Making (extended abstract)
authors: Marwa Abdulhai, Micah Carroll, Justin Svegliato, Anca Dragan, Sergey Levine
formalism: partially observed Markov decision processes; regret
formal_object: Communication POMDP between a speaker and a listener; the speaker is deceptive if the listener's regret is positive, i.e. acting on beliefs updated by the speaker yields lower expected reward than acting on its prior; task, belief and combined regret.
key_formula: Deceptive iff Regret(s, pi_L, pi_S) > 0: the listener's expected reward after interacting with S falls below what it would get acting on its prior belief b_L^0 (altruistic if negative, neutral if zero).
assumptions: A model of the listener (prior, model of the speaker's policy) and its reward; no beliefs or intentions of the speaker are required.
relevance: A deception definition based on harm to the listener rather than on intent; covers omissions and true-but-misleading statements, which matter for CoTs that mislead a monitor.

title: Higher-Order Belief in Incomplete Information MAIDs
authors: Jack Foxabbott, Rohan Subramani, Francis Rhys Ward
formalism: incomplete-information multi-agent influence diagrams; extensive-form games without a common prior
formal_object: II-MAIDs (infinite and finite depth) representing agents' beliefs about the game and about each other's beliefs; equivalence to incomplete-information EFGs; a recursive best-response solution concept.
assumptions: Known game structure; finite-depth belief hierarchies for the realistic solution concept.
relevance: Believing one is evaluated is the core of alignment faking and sandbagging; II-MAIDs give a formal language for 'behaves differently because it believes it is observed' (running example: an AI agent under evaluation).

title: Evaluating Language Model Character Traits
authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Zejia Yang, Alex Jackson, Randy Brown, Chandler Smith, Grace Colverd, Louis Thomson, Raymond Douglas, et al.
formalism: probabilistic behaviourism over context-response distributions
formal_object: A character trait measure maps tuples of context-response pairs to a score; an LM consistently exhibits a trait when the mean squared deviation from it is small; Ward et al.'s intention adapted to LMs; stationary and reflective traits.
key_formula: m:\bigcup_{n=0}^{N}(\mathcal C\times\mathcal R)^n\to\mathcal S,\quad m(\langle(c_0,r_0),\dots,(c_n,r_n)\rangle)=s
assumptions: An input distribution d(c); an external judgement of truth or harm; no access to internals.
relevance: Shows how to lift SCG belief and intention to an LM's input-output distribution; gives LM-level definitions of truthful and coherent beliefs, though mostly as measures.

title: A Causal Perspective on AI Deception in Games
authors: Francis Rhys Ward, Francesca Toni, Francesco Belardinelli
formalism: multi-agent influence models (MAIMs), Nash equilibrium
formal_object: Belief-free (functional) deception incentive: S has an incentive to signal V to T, and T's decision differs from the counterfactual model in which T observes V; a truthful policy makes T act as though it observed V.
key_formula: Def. 6, cond. 2: D^T(\pi^*)\neq D^T_{V\dashrightarrow D^T}(\pi^*_{-T},\pi^{BR}_T) for any best response \pi^{BR}_T in \mathcal M_{V\dashrightarrow D^T}
assumptions: Known MAIM; Nash equilibrium and best responses.
relevance: A belief-free variant, useful where ascribing beliefs to LLMs is contested; its truthfulness condition (the receiver acts as if it saw the truth) is directly comparable to a monitor reading a CoT. Superseded by the 2023 paper.

title: The Ditmarsch Tale of Wonders - The Dynamics of Lying
authors: Hans van Ditmarsch
venue: arXiv preprint (published in Synthese, 2014, per search record)
formalism: dynamic epistemic logic (belief modalities, action models)
formal_object: 'Lie that phi' as an action interpreted as a state transformer on pointed Kripke models of agents' beliefs; outside-observer versus agent-to-agent lies; credulous, skeptical and belief-revising addressees; complete axiomatisations.
assumptions: An explicit Kripke model of the agents' beliefs; lies as public or private announcements.
relevance: The logic tradition's formal definition of lying, including lies about others' beliefs; needs explicit belief models, so it applies to LLMs only after belief is fixed by another definition.

title: Toward a Formal Analysis of Deceptive Signaling
authors: Don Fallis, Peter J. Lewis
formalism: Lewisian sender-receiver signalling games
formal_object: Critique of Skyrms's formal analysis of functional deception (a misleading signal that benefits the sender) and of the alternatives of Godfrey-Smith and McWhirter; argues all three are seriously flawed.
assumptions: Signalling game with known payoffs and receiver updating.
relevance: Shows that definitions of deception without intent, based on misleading signals that benefit the sender, yield counterexamples; relevant if one defines LLM deception without ascribing beliefs.

title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision
authors: Collin Burns, Haotian Ye, Dan Klein, Jacob Steinhardt
formalism: unsupervised probing under logical-consistency constraints
formal_object: A direction in activation space satisfying logical consistency (a statement and its negation get opposite truth values), proposed as recovering the model's latent knowledge independently of its outputs.
assumptions: Access to activations; yes-no questions; consistency assumed to single out truth.
relevance: An operational criterion for what the model believes from internals, the ingredient a lying definition (output differs from belief) needs; it measures rather than defines belief.

title: How to Catch an AI Liar: Lie Detection in Black-Box LLMs by Asking Unrelated Questions
authors: Lorenzo Pacchiardi, Alex J. Chan, Soren Mindermann, Ilan Moscovitz, Alexa Y. Pan, Yarin Gal, Owain Evans, Jan Brauner
formalism: operational definition plus a logistic-regression detector
formal_object: A lie is outputting a false statement despite 'knowing' the truth in a demonstrable sense; detected from yes/no answers to unrelated follow-up questions.
assumptions: Demonstrable knowledge (the model answers correctly elsewhere); black-box access.
relevance: The common operational 'knows but says otherwise' definition of LLM lying; illustrates the gap between operational definitions and a formal account of belief.

title: AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations
authors: Teun van der Weij, Felix Hofstatter, Ollie Jaffe, Samuel F. Brown, Francis Rhys Ward
formalism: informal definition
formal_object: Sandbagging defined as strategic underperformance on an evaluation, by the developer or by the AI system itself.
assumptions: A notion of actual capability distinct from evaluated performance; a strategic motive.
relevance: The standard definition. Its 'strategic' clause could be formalised as SCG intention and 'underperformance' as a capability-performance gap; no formal version found.

title: Risks from Learned Optimization in Advanced Machine Learning Systems
authors: Evan Hubinger, Chris van Merwijk, Vladimir Mikulik, Joar Skalse, Scott Garrabrant
formalism: informal
formal_object: Mesa-optimisation: a learned model that is itself an optimiser, with a mesa-objective that may differ from the training loss; the origin of the deceptive-alignment concept.
assumptions: None formal.
relevance: Source of the scheming and deceptive-alignment concepts, all informal. Goal-directedness (MEG) and agent discovery are the closest formal follow-ups found.

title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ARC technical report)
authors: Paul Christiano, Mark Xu, Ajeya Cotra
venue: Alignment Research Center technical report (linkpost, Alignment Forum)
formalism: semi-formal problem statement
formal_object: The problem of learning to map an AI's model of the world to a human's model (ontology identification), i.e. training a reporter that states what the model knows rather than what a human would believe.
assumptions: A predictor with internal knowledge; a human-interpretable question space.
relevance: Frames honesty as reporting the model's own latent knowledge; semi-formal. The formal work building on it (CCS) is measurement-level.

title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
authors: Atticus Geiger, Duligur Ibeling, Amir Zur, Maheep Chaudhary, Sonakshi Chauhan, Jing Huang, Aryaman Arora, Zhengxuan Wu, Noah Goodman, Christopher Potts, Thomas Icard
venue: JMLR 26 (arXiv 2301.04709, first posted 2023 as 'Causal Abstraction for Faithful Model Interpretation')
formalism: causal abstraction over deterministic causal models with intervention algebras (hard, soft and functional interventionals)
formal_object: Exact transformation and constructive abstraction (high-level H faithful to low-level L under alignment); approximate transformation as graded faithfulness (Sec. 3.2); interchange intervention accuracy (Def. 48); LIME read as behavioural-only approximate abstraction.
key_formula: \tau\big(\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{I}})\big)=\mathrm{Solve}\big(\mathcal{M}^*_{\omega(\mathbf{I})}\big);\quad \mathbb{S}_{\mathbf{I}\sim\mathbb{P}}\big[\mathrm{Sim}\big(\tau(\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{I}})),\mathrm{Solve}(\mathcal{M}^*_{\omega(\mathbf{I})})\big)\big]\ge\eta;\quad \mathrm{IIA}=\mathbb{E}_{i\sim P}\,\mathbb{1}[\mathrm{Proj}_{X^{Out}_H}(\tau^\pi(L_i))=\mathrm{Proj}_{X^{Out}_H}(H_{\omega^\pi(i)})]
assumptions: White-box low-level model (full access to internals and the ability to intervene); a proposed high-level model; an alignment (partition plus value maps); a distribution over interventions, a similarity function and a summary statistic for the graded version.
relevance: The reference formal definition of a faithful explanation as a simplification of the computation. It states that graded faithfulness has no single correct metric. A CoT could be cast as the high-level model H.

title: Approximate Causal Abstraction
authors: Sander Beckers, Frederick Eberhardt, Joseph Y. Halpern
formalism: structural causal models (Halpern-Pearl style deterministic and probabilistic causal models)
formal_object: tau-alpha-approximate abstraction: worst-case distance, over allowed low-level interventions and contexts, between lifting the low-level outcome via tau and running the high-level model on the lifted intervention. alpha = 0 recovers exact tau-abstraction.
key_formula: d_\tau(M_L,M_H)=\min_{\tau_U}\max_{\vec X\leftarrow\vec x\in\mathcal{I}_L,\ \vec u_L\in\mathcal{R}_L(\mathcal{U}_L)} d_{\mathcal{V}_H}\big(\tau(M_L(\vec u_L,\vec X\leftarrow\vec x)),\ M_H(\tau_U(\vec u_L),\omega_\tau(\vec X\leftarrow\vec x))\big);\ M_H\ \text{is a }\tau\text{-}\alpha\text{ approximate abstraction iff } d_\tau\le\alpha
assumptions: Known low- and high-level causal models; a surjective state map tau; a metric on high-level states; extended to probabilistic models with a distance over distributions.
relevance: Gives a worst-case graded faithfulness grounded in the Halpern-Pearl causal-model formalism. It is the most direct bridge to the user's actual-causality plans.

title: Abstracting Causal Models
authors: Sander Beckers, Joseph Y. Halpern
formalism: structural causal models (Halpern-Pearl)
formal_object: A hierarchy: exact transformation, then uniform transformation, then tau-abstraction (the intervention map omega is induced by the state map tau), then strong and constructive tau-abstraction. These are binary relations stating when a coarse model faithfully abstracts a fine one.
key_formula: (M_H,\mathcal{I}_H)\ \text{is a }\tau\text{-abstraction of }(M_L,\mathcal{I}_L)\ \text{iff }\tau\ \text{surjective},\ \exists\,\tau_U\ \text{surjective with}\ \tau(M_L(\vec u_L,\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y))=M_H(\tau_U(\vec u_L),\omega_\tau(\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y))\ \forall\,\vec Y\leftarrow\vec y\in\mathcal{I}_L,\ \text{and}\ \mathcal{I}_H=\omega_\tau(\mathcal{I}_L)
assumptions: Known deterministic or probabilistic causal models; the set of allowed low-level interventions; a surjective state map.
relevance: Supplies the exact (binary) faithfulness relation in Halpern's framework. It is what any approximate notion reduces to at zero error, and it composes with HP actual causality.

title: Causal Consistency of Structural Equation Models
authors: Paul K. Rubenstein, Sebastian Weichwald, Stephan Bongers, Joris M. Mooij, Dominik Janzing, Moritz Grosse-Wentrup, Bernhard Schölkopf
formalism: structural equation models, interventional distributions
formal_object: Exact (tau-omega) transformation between SEMs: two models are causally consistent if they agree on the effects of all (well-specified) interventions after mapping states and interventions.
assumptions: Probabilistic SEMs; a state map tau and an order-preserving intervention map omega; a chosen set of interventions.
relevance: The original consistency criterion on which every later abstraction-based faithfulness definition builds. Geiger's exact transformation is a variant of it.

title: Causal Abstraction Inference under Lossy Representations
authors: Kevin Xia, Elias Bareinboim
formalism: structural causal models, Pearl's causal hierarchy, graphical identification
formal_object: Projected abstractions, which drop the abstract invariance condition so that many low-level interventions with different effects may map to one high-level intervention. Includes translation of observational, interventional and counterfactual queries and a graphical criterion for identifying them.
assumptions: A low-level SCM or limited low-level data; a (lossy) abstraction function; graphical assumptions for identification.
relevance: Verbalizing reasoning is lossy: many internal states map to one CoT step. Standard abstraction is ill-defined there, so this is the needed extension for a CoT-as-abstraction definition.

title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
authors: Denis Sutter, Julian Minder, Thomas Hofmann, Tiago Pimentel
formalism: causal abstraction with arbitrary alignment maps; impossibility result
formal_object: Proves that, under reasonable assumptions and with unrestricted (non-linear) alignment maps, any network can be mapped to any algorithm. It reaches 100% IIA even on randomly initialised LMs.
assumptions: Arbitrarily powerful alignment maps; the paper's stated regularity assumptions.
relevance: Any causal-abstraction definition of CoT faithfulness must restrict the class of alignment maps (an information-encoding assumption). Otherwise faithfulness is vacuous.

title: Everything, Everywhere, All at Once: Is Mechanistic Interpretability Identifiable?
authors: Maxime Méloux, Silviu Maniu, François Portet, Maxime Peyrard
formalism: statistical identifiability applied to causal-alignment explanations (exhaustive enumeration)
formal_object: Asks whether a unique explanation exists under mechanistic-interpretability criteria. Shows systematic non-identifiability: several circuits, several interpretations per circuit, several algorithms per network and several subspaces per algorithm.
assumptions: Small MLPs on Boolean functions; full enumeration of candidate circuits and alignments.
relevance: Faithfulness defined as abstraction does not single out one explanation. A CoT could be faithful alongside incompatible rival explanations, so the definition must say whether it requires uniqueness.

title: Validating Causal Abstraction Metrics on Simulated Complex Systems
authors: Maxime Méloux, Tiago Pimentel, François Portet, Maxime Peyrard
formalism: causal abstraction; benchmark of more than 30 observational, information-theoretic and causal metrics
formal_object: Causal Abstraction Error (CAE): a continuous validity metric for a high-level explanation that includes an explicit faithfulness test over unmapped low-level variables.
assumptions: Systems with ground-truth high-level explanations; the ability to intervene on mapped and unmapped variables.
relevance: Finds that only causal metrics separate valid from invalid abstractions, and only if unmapped variables are tested. That test is a formal handle on explanation completeness, the part a CoT leaves out.

title: Compositional Abstraction Error and a Category of Causal Models
authors: Eigil F. Rischel, Sebastian Weichwald
formalism: category theory (enriched categories) over finite interventional causal models
formal_object: A category of finite interventional causal models whose abstraction errors compose: the error of an M to M'' abstraction is bounded by the sum of the step errors.
assumptions: Finite interventional causal models; a chosen distance between distributions.
relevance: A compositionality desideratum for graded faithfulness. It is useful if CoT faithfulness is defined through a chain of abstractions (network to features to verbal steps).

title: CAuSE: Decoding Multimodal Classifiers using Faithful Natural Language Explanation
authors: Dibyanayan Bandyopadhyay, Soham Bhattacharjee, Mohammed Hasanuzzaman, Asif Ekbal
formalism: causal abstraction via interchange intervention training (IIT)
formal_object: A natural-language explainer trained by interchange intervention against a frozen classifier. Theorem 1: under idealized conditions (identical weights and an injective encoder) the explainer is a causal abstraction of the classifier and vice versa. Also a causal-faithfulness metric.
assumptions: White-box access to the classifier; an idealized two-neuron linear setting for the Lemma; an injective encoder.
relevance: The only work found that ties natural-language explanations to causal abstraction formally. It does so for classifiers, not for an LLM's own CoT.

title: Position: Causality is Key for Interpretability Claims to Generalise
authors: Shruti Joshi, Aaron Mueller, David Klindt, Wieland Brendel, Patrik Reizinger, Dhanya Sridhar
venue: arXiv preprint (seed list says ICML; the arXiv page gives no venue)
formalism: Pearl's causal hierarchy; identifiability up to equivalence class; causal representation learning
formal_object: Informally defines estimand, equivalence class and identifiability (estimand constant within a class, varying across classes). Maps interpretability claims to rungs L1-L3. Separates ontological faithfulness from instrumental adequacy (App. B.5). No theorem.
assumptions: A stated estimand and intervention class; CRL assumptions for recovering variables from activations.
relevance: Gives the vocabulary for a CoT-faithfulness definition. Faithfulness claims about what the model would have output are rung-3 counterfactuals, mostly unverifiable without controlled supervision. Also separates ontological from instrumental faithfulness.

title: Causal Differentiating Concepts: Interpreting LM Behavior via Causal Representation Learning
authors: Navita Goyal, Hal Daumé III, Alexandre Drouin, Dhanya Sridhar
formalism: causal representation learning; interchange interventions; identifiability theory
formal_object: Causal differentiating concept (Def. 2): a latent whose interchange intervention is necessary and sufficient to switch behaviour k to l. Latents identified up to affine maps (logit-linear assumption), and up to permutation and scaling with 1-sparsity.
key_formula: \text{(nec.) } \forall x_k\in C_k,x_l\in C_l:\ M_{z_k^s\leftarrow z_l^s}(x_k)\neq c_l\ (s\neq r);\quad \text{(suff.) } \exists x_k\in C_k,x_l\in C_l:\ M_{z_k^r\leftarrow z_l^r}(x_k)=c_l
assumptions: Access to LM activations; behaviour logit-linear in the latent concepts; 1-sparse concept differences between behaviour groups.
relevance: Gives a necessary-and-sufficient interchange criterion and conditions under which behaviour-driving concept variables are identifiable in LMs. These are the ground-truth variables a faithful CoT would have to mention.

title: Sparse Shift Autoencoders for Identifying Concepts from Large Language Model Activations
authors: Shruti Joshi, Andrea Dittadi, Sébastien Lachapelle, Dhanya Sridhar
venue: arXiv preprint (cited by the position paper as 'Identifiable steering via sparse autoencoding of multi-concept shifts')
formalism: causal representation learning; identifiability from paired observations
formal_object: Sparse Shift Autoencoders: sparse representations of embedding differences. Proved identifiable from paired observations that differ in multiple unknown concepts, but not all.
assumptions: Paired prompts differing in a sparse, unknown subset of concepts; access to activations.
relevance: Gives identifiability conditions for concept variables in real LLM activations. These are needed before 'the CoT reports the concepts the model used' can have a well-defined truth value.

title: Unsupervised Causal Abstractions Discovery
authors: Théo Saulus, Simon Lacoste-Julien, Dhanya Sridhar
venue: arXiv preprint (seed list says UAI 2026 workshop)
formalism: causal abstraction; low-rank causal discovery; factor SCMs
formal_object: Thm 1: latents of a low-rank (factor) graph form a uniform transformation (abstraction) of the low-level SCM. Thms 2-3: factor graph and linear mechanisms identifiable up to permutation and affine maps. Thm 4 bounds approximate-transformation error.
key_formula: \mathbb{E}_{i\sim P,\,u\sim\Pr}\big[d_H\big(\tau(\mathrm{Solve}(L_i;u)),\mathrm{Solve}(H_{\omega(i)};u)\big)\big]\le\eta
assumptions: Low-level data generated by a factor SCM with a bipartite, strongly acyclic graph; anchors; linear parent mechanisms; Lipschitz mechanisms for the bound.
relevance: Learns the high-level model rather than testing a proposed one, with identifiability guarantees. This is a route to a reference abstraction against which a CoT could be compared.

title: Interpretability is in the Mind of the Beholder: A Causal Framework for Human-interpretable Representation Learning
authors: Emanuele Marconato, Andrea Passerini, Stefano Teso
formalism: causal representation learning with the human as an external observer; information-theoretic reformulation
formal_object: Alignment between a machine representation and the human's concept vocabulary, linked to interpretability through a 'name transfer' game. Disentanglement, concept leakage and content-style separation are recast information-theoretically.
assumptions: A causal model of the human's concepts and of the machine's representation; an observer model.
relevance: Adds the human receiver to the causal picture. This is needed to extend an abstraction-based faithfulness definition to legibility and simulatability, where the CoT must be readable by the reader as well as faithful.

title: Causal Abstractions of Neural Networks
authors: Atticus Geiger, Hanson Lu, Thomas Icard, Christopher Potts
formalism: causal abstraction; interchange interventions
formal_object: Aligns neural representations with variables of an interpretable causal model and uses interchange interventions to verify that they have the causal properties of the aligned variables.
assumptions: White-box network; a candidate high-level causal model; a hand-chosen alignment.
relevance: The first operational use of causal abstraction for neural networks. It is superseded formally by Geiger et al. 2025 and listed for completeness.

title: From Isolation to Entanglement: When Do Interpretability Methods Identify and Disentangle Known Concepts?
authors: Aaron Mueller, Andrew Lee, Shruti Joshi, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Dhanya Sridhar, Patrik Reizinger
formalism: identifiability metrics (MCC, DCI-ES); steering selectivity
formal_object: An empirical multi-concept evaluation. It uses standard identifiability definitions (weak identifiability, identifiability up to elementwise nonlinearity, App. C) and tests whether SAEs and probes recover and selectively steer correlated concepts. No new concept definition.
assumptions: Known ground-truth concepts with controlled correlations; access to activations.
relevance: Shows that features look disentangled correlationally but steering is not selective. Concept-level faithfulness claims therefore need interventional, multi-concept tests.

title: Who Guards the Guardians? The Challenges of Evaluating Identifiability of Learned Representations
authors: Shruti Joshi, Théo Saulus, Wieland Brendel, Philippe Brouillard, Dhanya Sridhar, Patrik Reizinger
formalism: identifiability theory; metric validity analysis
formal_object: Defines identifiability up to a transformation class G (permutation-scaling, affine, elementwise nonlinear) and extends it to dimension mismatch. Proves that MCC and DCI give false positives or negatives outside their implicit assumptions (Props. 1-3).
key_formula: f\circ g=h,\quad h\in\mathcal{G}
assumptions: Known data-generating process and encoder geometry; m = d for the basic definition.
relevance: Warns that identifiability metrics are themselves misspecified outside their assumptions. This matters for any empirical check of a concept-level faithfulness definition.

title: Three Desiderata for Faithfulness in Machine Learning Explanations: The Case for Causal Abstraction
authors: Mette Friis Andersen, Maria Heuss, Ana Lucic
formalism: causal abstraction (position)
formal_object: Three desiderata for faithfulness (reverse-engineering specific behaviors, interventionist causal relations, appropriate model decomposition), argued to be met by causal abstraction.
assumptions: Adopts the causal abstraction framework; no new formal definition.
relevance: States explicitly that there is no agreed definition of faithfulness and argues for causal abstraction as the evaluation framework.
verified: abstract (opened in a browser; OpenReview blocks automated fetches)

title: A Decision-Theoretic Formalisation of Steganography With Applications to LLM Monitoring
authors: Usman Anwar, Julianna Piskorz, David D. Baek, David Africa, Jim Weatherall, Max Tegmark, Christian Schroeder de Witt, Mihaela van der Schaar, David Krueger
formalism: decision theory; generalised V-information (usable information relative to a decoder class)
formal_object: Steganographic gap: the usable information a signal Z gives a Receiver decoder class minus what it gives a trusted Sentinel class, on an auditing task (Y,u). Z counts as steganographic iff the gap is positive.
key_formula: \Delta_{\mathrm{steg}}(Z)=I_{\mathrm{rec}}(Z\to Y)-I_{\mathrm{sen}}(Z\to Y),\quad I^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\to Y\mid X)=U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z)-U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X),\quad U^{u}_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)=\sup_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbb{E}[u(Y,d[X])]
assumptions: Decoder classes V_rec and V_sen; a Sentinel matched in capability but without the key; an auditing task with ground truth Y and utility u; observable downstream decisions. No covertext distribution needed.
relevance: The only definition of steganographic reasoning that needs no reference distribution. Steganography is relative to a monitor class and a task. Recovers Cachin's epsilon-security as a special case (App. D). Template for monitor-relative definitions.

title: A Theory of Usable Information Under Computational Constraints
authors: Yilun Xu, Shengjia Zhao, Jiaming Song, Russell Stewart, Stefano Ermon
formalism: variational information theory (predictive V-information)
formal_object: Predictive V-information: the reduction in the best log loss that a constrained predictor family V gets from seeing Z. Unlike Shannon information, it can be created by computation and destroyed by encryption.
key_formula: I_{\mathcal{V}}(Z\to Y\mid X)=H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)-H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X,Z),\quad H_{\mathcal{V}}(Y\mid X)=\inf_{d\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbb{E}[-\log d[X](Y)] \text{ (as restated in arXiv 2602.23163, Eqs. 1-3)}
assumptions: A predictive family V that satisfies optional ignorance; a joint distribution over (X, Y, Z); log loss, or a utility in the generalised version.
relevance: The common primitive behind monitor-relative monitorability (Anwar et al. 2026, App. E), the steganographic gap and REV (in the map). Lets 'illegible' and 'encoded' be defined as information that exists but is not usable by a monitor class.

title: Analyzing and Improving Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Information Theory
authors: Usman Anwar, Tim Bakker, Dana Kianfar, Cristina Pinneri, Christos Louizos
formalism: information theory; Bayes-optimal monitors; V-information (App. E)
formal_object: CoT monitorability of an attribute Y: the accuracy uplift of the Bayes-optimal CoT monitor over the prompt-only monitor. Bounded by conditional MI. A practical monitor's error splits into information gap and elicitation error.
key_formula: \delta:=\alpha_{\text{CoT}}-\alpha_{\text{Prompt}},\quad 0\leq\delta\leq\sqrt{2I(Y;Z|X)};\quad I_{\mathcal{V}}(Y;Z\mid X):=\inf_{h\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(Y,h(X))]-\inf_{h\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbb{E}[\ell(Y,h(X,Z))]
assumptions: A ground-truth output monitor g that defines the attribute; the policy distribution pi(O|X,Z); a monitor hypothesis class V for the practical version.
relevance: The closest existing concept-level formal definition of CoT monitorability, relative to an attribute and (in App. E) to a monitor class. Purely observational: MI > 0 is satisfied by post-hoc CoTs too (Remark 3.11).

title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
authors: Bowen Baker, Joost Huizinga, Leo Gao, Zehao Dou, Melody Y. Guan, Aleksander Madry, Wojciech Zaremba, Jakub Pachocki, David Farhi
formalism: statistics (sufficient statistic); monitor-relative recoverability
formal_object: A latent z (e.g. a CoT) is faithful w.r.t. output property v iff z is a sufficient statistic for v. It is legible to monitor M iff M can predict v from z. Monitor success implies both.
assumptions: A target property v of outputs; a joint distribution over latent and output; a specific monitor M for legibility. Stated verbally in §5.1, with no formula.
relevance: Splits monitorability into a monitor-free part (sufficiency, faithfulness) and a monitor-relative part (legibility). This is the same split as Shannon information vs V-information, and the natural starting point for a causal refinement.

title: Hidden Reasoning Must Leak, but Need Not Be Readable: Fundamental Opportunities and Limits for Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
authors: Mohammadali Mohammadkhani, Madhava Krishna, Yash Sarrof, Michael Hahn
formalism: circuit complexity of fixed-precision transformers; information theory; cryptography (NC0 pseudo-random generators)
formal_object: Information-theoretic footprint I[X_covert; CoT] of covert computation. Thm 3.1: beyond model capacity the footprint must be near-linear. Thm 3.5: a 1-layer transformer can encrypt its CoT so that no polynomial-time monitor beats chance.
key_formula: I[X_{\mathrm{covert}},\mathrm{CoT}]=\tilde{\Omega}(N)\ \text{whenever }|\mathrm{CoT}|\text{ is polynomially bounded in }N:=|X_{\mathrm{covert}}|\ \text{(Eq. 3, transcribed from PDF)}
assumptions: Fixed-precision transformer; specific state-tracking and arithmetic tasks with a uniform covert input; greedy decoding; Thm 3.5 needs an unproven NC0 PRG assumption.
relevance: Formally separates leakage (Shannon) from readability (computationally bounded monitors). A definition of monitorability or encoded reasoning must therefore be relative to a monitor class, not stated in raw mutual information.

title: An Information-Theoretic Model for Steganography
authors: Christian Cachin
venue: Information Hiding Workshop 1998; revised version in Information and Computation (2004)
formalism: information theory; hypothesis testing
formal_object: Security of a stegosystem against a passive warden: the relative entropy between covertext and stegotext distributions, which bounds any detector. epsilon-secure if it is at most epsilon, perfectly secure if it is zero.
key_formula: D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{1}\|P_{0})\leq\varepsilon\ \text{(as restated in arXiv 2602.23163, App. D; the abstract states the relative entropy between the distributions of } C \text{ and } S)
assumptions: A known covertext distribution; a passive adversary; the detection task framed as hypothesis testing.
relevance: The classical security definition. Encoded-reasoning definitions must either supply a covertext distribution (an 'honest CoT' distribution, unavailable for LLMs) or replace it, as the decision-theoretic gap does.

title: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs
authors: Jan Hendrik Kirchner, Yining Chen, Harri Edwards, Jan Leike, Nat McAleese, Yuri Burda
formalism: interactive-proof-style completeness and soundness relative to a verifier and a prover model family
formal_object: Checkability (verifiability) of prover pi to verifier v on P_XY. Completeness: correct outputs are accepted. Soundness: no prover in family H gets an incorrect output accepted. Legibility is checkability in practice.
key_formula: \text{Completeness: }\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\ \mathds{1}_{\text{correct}}(x,\pi(x))=v(x,\pi(x))=1;\quad \text{Soundness: }\forall\pi^{\prime}\in\mathcal{H},\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\ \mathds{1}_{\text{correct}}(x,\pi^{\prime}(x))=0\implies v(x,\pi^{\prime}(x))=0
assumptions: A ground-truth correctness label; a verifier class (small models or time-limited humans); an adversarial prover family H.
relevance: The standard formal definition of legibility/checkability for CoT. It concerns correctness of the answer, not whether the CoT reflects the computation. Contrasting it with faithfulness is needed.

title: Opacity in Discrete Event Systems: A Perspective and Overview
authors: Xiang Yin
formalism: partially observed automata; state estimation; hyperproperties (HyperLTL)
formal_object: Opacity: an observer can never know for sure that the system is, was, or will be in a secret state (current-state, initial-state, K-step variants). Diagnosability is the dual: a fault is always inferred within finite delay.
assumptions: A known system model (automaton or Petri net); an observation map such as a natural projection; a secret set of states or language; worst-case (possibilistic) or stochastic inference.
relevance: A mature formal framework that covers several concepts at once. Diagnosability is formal monitorability ('always eventually know'), opacity is formal obfuscation ('always not know'), and both are unified as hyperproperties. Points to Lin 2011 and Sampath et al. 1995.

title: Provably Secure Steganography
authors: Nicholas J. Hopper, John Langford, Luis von Ahn
venue: CRYPTO 2002 (extended abstract); full version IACR ePrint 2002/137
formalism: complexity theory; computational indistinguishability
formal_object: Steganographic security against a computationally bounded warden: stegotexts are computationally indistinguishable from covertexts drawn from a channel. Secure stegosystems exist if one-way functions exist.
assumptions: Sampling access to the covertext channel; a shared secret key; polynomial-time adversaries.
relevance: The computational counterpart of Cachin. With Mohammadkhani et al. it shows that undetectability by bounded monitors is the relevant notion for encoded CoT. It still needs a cover distribution and a shared key.

title: Perfectly Secure Steganography Using Minimum Entropy Coupling
authors: Christian Schroeder de Witt, Samuel Sokota, J. Zico Kolter, Jakob Foerster, Martin Strohmeier
formalism: information theory (couplings, minimum entropy coupling)
formal_object: Characterization: a steganography procedure is perfectly secure under Cachin's model iff it is induced by a coupling. Among those, it maximizes throughput iff induced by a minimum entropy coupling.
assumptions: Cachin's model with a known covertext distribution, here given by a generative model such as GPT-2; a shared key.
relevance: Shows that perfectly undetectable encoding in LLM text is achievable. Distribution-based detection of encoded reasoning therefore cannot work in principle, which motivates behavioural, monitor-relative definitions.

title: Learning to Give Checkable Answers with Prover-Verifier Games
authors: Cem Anil, Guodong Zhang, Yuhuai Wu, Roger Grosse
formalism: game theory (simultaneous and sequential prover-verifier games, Stackelberg equilibria)
formal_object: Prover-Verifier Games. A trusted verifier and an untrusted, stronger prover with competing objectives. Identifies the game variants whose equilibria provably yield a sound and complete justification protocol.
assumptions: A decision problem with ground truth; learner classes for prover and verifier; equilibrium play.
relevance: The game-theoretic source of Kirchner's checkability definition. It defines checkable answers as an equilibrium property, which fits a definition of legibility relative to a verifier class.

title: Models That Prove Their Own Correctness
authors: Noga Amit, Shafi Goldwasser, Orr Paradise, Guy Rothblum
formalism: interactive proofs; learning theory
formal_object: Self-Proving model: w.h.p. over inputs from a distribution, it outputs a correct answer and convinces verifier V via an interactive proof. V's soundness guarantees that no model can convince it of an incorrect output on any input.
assumptions: A verification algorithm V with an interactive proof for the task (e.g. GCD); an input distribution; accepting transcripts or verifier feedback for training.
relevance: The most rigorous formalization of checkability for learned models: soundness holds for every input and every prover, not just on average. Gives a crypto-grade target for a 'checkable CoT' definition.

title: AI safety via debate
authors: Geoffrey Irving, Paul Christiano, Dario Amodei
formalism: complexity theory (interactive proofs); zero-sum games
formal_object: Debate: a zero-sum game between two agents judged by a human. With optimal play, debate with polynomial-time judges answers any PSPACE question (direct judging answers only NP).
assumptions: Optimal play; an honest debater able to simulate the computation; a polynomial-time judge.
relevance: Frames oversight as which problem classes a weak judge can verify. This is a complexity-theoretic notion of checkability that can be adapted to judge monitorability.

title: Avoiding Obfuscation with Prover-Estimator Debate
authors: Jonah Brown-Cohen, Geoffrey Irving, Georgios Piliouras, Lijie Chen, Jiawei Li, Zhiyang Xun
formalism: complexity theory; recursive debate protocols
formal_object: The obfuscated arguments problem: a dishonest debater forces an honest one into an intractable check. A prover-estimator protocol lets the honest debater win with efficiency comparable to the opponent, under stability assumptions.
assumptions: Recursive problem decomposition; stability assumptions on the subclaim probabilities; computationally bounded debaters.
relevance: The only formal treatment of argument obfuscation, meaning obfuscation by intractability rather than hiding. Relevant to defining obfuscated CoT relative to a verifier's computational budget.

title: Games for AI Control: Models of Safety Evaluations of AI Deployment Protocols
authors: Charlie Griffin, Louis Thomson, Buck Shlegeris, Alessandro Abate
formalism: game theory (multi-objective partially observable stochastic games)
formal_object: AI-Control Games between a protocol designer and a red team, which controls a scheming untrusted model. Safety and usefulness of protocols such as Trusted Monitoring are defined as game values, with reductions to zero-sum POSGs.
assumptions: A scheming untrusted model that knows the protocol; a trusted weaker monitor; a limited human audit budget; specified payoffs.
relevance: Formalizes oversight as a game against an adversarial policy. It suggests defining monitorability as safety achievable by a monitor class against a worst-case policy class, not on average.

title: Monitorability of omega-regular languages
authors: Andreas Bauer
formalism: formal languages; temporal logic (LTL); runtime verification
formal_object: Runtime-verification monitorability: a property L is monitorable iff every finite prefix u has a finite extension v after which every infinite continuation is in L, or every one is outside L. Gives the complexity of deciding it.
key_formula: \forall u\,\exists v:\ (\forall w.\ uvw\in L)\ \lor\ (\forall w.\ uvw\notin L)\ \text{(rendered from the abstract)}
assumptions: A specification given as an omega-regular language or LTL formula; observation of finite prefixes of an execution.
relevance: 'Monitorability' already has a precise meaning in formal methods: verdict-determinability from finite observation. The CoT notion differs (inference of a hidden property), so the terminology clash should be addressed.

title: Legibility and Predictability of Robot Motion
authors: Anca D. Dragan, Kenton C.T. Lee, Siddhartha S. Srinivasa
formalism: Bayesian goal inference (inverse planning with a cost-based observer model)
formal_object: Legibility: the observer infers the correct goal quickly and confidently from a trajectory prefix (action-to-goal inference). Predictability: the trajectory matches the observer's goal-to-action expectation. The two can conflict.
key_formula: \mathrm{legibility}(\xi)=\frac{\int P(G^{*}\mid\xi_{S\to\xi(t)})\,f(t)\,dt}{\int f(t)\,dt}\ \text{(Eq. 9; transcribed from PDF)}
assumptions: A known goal set; an observer model of rational action with cost function C; a time-weighting f(t).
relevance: A formal, observer-relative definition of legibility as speed of correct intent inference from a partial trace. It maps directly onto monitoring a CoT prefix for the model's goal. Its legibility/predictability split parallels legibility vs simulatability.

title: A Unified Framework for Planning in Adversarial and Cooperative Environments
authors: Anagha Kulkarni, Siddharth Srivastava, Subbarao Kambhampati
formalism: classical planning with a partially informed observer (observation model, belief over goals)
formal_object: Goal obfuscation: the plan's observations stay consistent with at least k goals. Goal legibility: they are consistent with at most j goals. Plan obfuscation and plan legibility control what the observer can infer about next actions.
assumptions: A known observer sensor model mapping action-state pairs to observations; a set of candidate (decoy or confounding) goals; an offline observer.
relevance: One framework that formally defines obfuscation and legibility as two ends of the same observer-relative quantity. A model for treating CoT obfuscation and legibility jointly.

title: Learning to Be Monitored: Causal Bounds and Intervention-Aware Post-Training Recipes for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
authors: Qiang Fu, Xinyue Li, Andre Wibisono, Arman Cohan
in_map: anon2026improving (likely the same work under a new title; OpenReview version in the map)
formalism: structural causal models; potential outcomes; partial identification bounds
formal_object: Causal recall: the probability that the monitor flags a case whose target outcome was caused by the intervention (Y(1)=1, Y(0)=0). The common TPR_mc metric is an upper bound, and a lower bound is derived.
assumptions: One SCM for both arms, with consistency (Assumption 1); a binary intervention; a binary outcome and monitor decision; p1 > p0.
relevance: The only causal (SCM/potential-outcome) definition of a monitorability quantity found. It already uses 'necessary cause' structure (Y(0)=0, Y(1)=1) and is directly extensible with Halpern-Pearl actual causation.

title: Don't Judge an Agent by Its Messages: Private-State Leakage under Passive Monitoring of Agent Communication
authors: Daksh Pandey, Sayon Duttagupta, Xinhai Zou, Amit Singh Bhati
formalism: information theory; partial identification of mutual-information leakage from observable laws
formal_object: What a passive auditor can certify about the leakage of private state through messages. Compatible MI leakage forms a sharp interval. It is determined iff the residual private state or the message is a deterministic function of the task state.
assumptions: The auditor knows the authorised sender and the exact observable message and outcome law, with no trusted pairing of messages and private states.
relevance: A formal non-identifiability result: matching an honest sender's observable behaviour cannot rule out covert leakage. It limits any observational, monitor-based definition of steganography.

title: Quantifying the Necessity of Chain of Thought through Opaque Serial Depth
authors: Jonah Brown-Cohen, David Lindner, Rohin Shah
formalism: circuit complexity (circuit depth between designated interpretable nodes)
formal_object: Opaque serial depth: the length of the longest computation possible without passing through interpretable nodes such as CoT tokens, computed as circuit depth between interpretable nodes. Bounds how much reasoning can stay unexternalized.
assumptions: A user-specified set of interpretable nodes; the paper admits there is no precise definition of interpretable and suggests monitorability evaluations or training-incentive arguments.
relevance: Formalizes the 'CoT is necessary' premise of monitorability arguments. Its dependence on an undefined 'interpretable' node set shows where a formal legibility definition is missing.

title: Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography
authors: Sumeet Ramesh Motwani, Mikhail Baranchuk, Martin Strohmeier, Vijay Bolina, Philip H. S. Torr, Lewis Hammond, Christian Schroeder de Witt
formalism: security concepts (Cachin/Hopper-style steganography) in a multi-agent setting
formal_object: Formalizes secret collusion among generative agents using steganography, the incentives for it, and the capabilities it requires. The abstract describes a formalisation and an evaluation framework, not a new security definition.
assumptions: Communicating LLM agents; an overseer of a shared channel.
relevance: Imports classical steganographic security into LLM multi-agent settings. Useful framing; the precise definitions should be checked in the full text.

title: Preventing Language Models From Hiding Their Reasoning
authors: Fabien Roger, Ryan Greenblatt
formalism: information theory (channel capacity)
formal_object: Encoded reasoning is defined informally (intermediate steps encoded in a way not understandable to readers). Formal only as the capacity of the encoder-paraphraser-decoder channel, used to evaluate paraphrasing defenses.
key_formula: I(M,\hat{M})=H(M)-H(M|\hat{M})=H(\hat{M})-H(\hat{M}|M)
assumptions: A known payload M and a decoder; a paraphraser defense.
relevance: Source of the encoded-reasoning concept. Its formal part measures hidden-message capacity, not whether hidden content is used as reasoning.

title: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Debate
authors: Jonah Brown-Cohen, Geoffrey Irving, Georgios Piliouras
formalism: complexity theory (doubly-efficient interactive proofs)
formal_object: Debate protocols in which the honest strategy needs only polynomially many simulation steps while verifying stochastic AI systems, even against a dishonest debater using exponentially many steps.
assumptions: Access to simulate the AI system; a polynomial-time judge.
relevance: Refines Irving et al. toward realistic computational costs. Superseded for obfuscation by prover-estimator debate.

title: Framework for Evaluating Faithfulness of Local Explanations
authors: Sanjoy Dasgupta, Nave Frost, Michal Moshkovitz
formalism: probability, learning theory (estimators, sample complexity)
formal_object: Faithfulness of an explanation system (f,e) split into consistency (same explanation implies same prediction) and sufficiency (any instance satisfying the explanation gets the same prediction), local and global, w.r.t. a data distribution.
key_formula: m^c(x)=\Pr_{x'\in_\mu C_\pi}\big(f(x')=f(x)\big),\ C_\pi=\{x\in\mathcal{X}: e(x)=\pi\};\quad m^s(x)=\Pr_{x'\in_\mu C_x}\big(f(x')=f(x)\big),\ C_x=\{x'\in\mathcal{X}: A(x',e(x))\}
assumptions: Input distribution mu; black-box access to f; 'intelligible' explanations with a checkable applicability relation A(x,pi); judges only outputs, not the internal process.
relevance: Closest formal concept-level definition of faithfulness that is agnostic to explanation format: a free-text rationale works as pi if A is judgeable. Consistency equals Gibbs-decoder accuracy, which links faithfulness, simulatability and checkability.

title: Impossibility Theorems for Feature Attribution
authors: Blair Bilodeau, Natasha Jaques, Pang Wei Koh, Been Kim
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 121(2)
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: hypothesis testing over model classes (statistical decision theory)
formal_object: Theorems: for moderately rich model classes, any complete and linear attribution method (IG, SHAP) can provably fail to beat random guessing at end-tasks such as local behaviour, spurious features and recourse.
assumptions: Attribution is complete and linear; model class rich enough (satisfied by neural nets); end-task framed as a hypothesis test about model behaviour.
relevance: Shows faithfulness is only well defined relative to a concrete end-task or inference. Suggests defining CoT faithfulness by what an observer can correctly infer about behaviour, not by axioms on the explanation.

title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
authors: Jack Lindsey
formalism: semi-formal interventionist causal criteria (tested by concept injection)
formal_object: Introspective awareness: a self-report that is accurate, grounded (causally depends on the described state), internal (the influence does not route through sampled outputs) and drawn from a metacognitive representation of the state.
assumptions: White-box access; the internal state must be identifiable and intervenable (e.g. as an injected concept vector); the metacognitive-representation criterion is not operationalized.
relevance: Grounding is counterfactual dependence ('if the internal state were different, the description would change accordingly'), and internality is a path-specific condition excluding paths through generated tokens. Both translate directly into SCM or Halpern-Pearl terms.

title: Privileged Self-Access Matters for Introspection in AI
authors: Siyuan Song, Harvey Lederman, Jennifer Hu, Kyle Mahowald
formalism: semi-formal, resource-bounded comparison with third-party observers
formal_object: Introspection: any process yielding information about internal states that is more reliable than any process of equal or lower computational cost available to a third party.
assumptions: A reliability measure, a ground-truth internal state, and a class of third-party processes bounded by computational cost.
relevance: Makes introspection relative to a compute-bounded observer class, the same structure as usable (V-)information and monitor-relative monitorability. It is a natural bridge to formalize introspection and monitorability in one framework. Lindsey endorses it over the lightweight definition.

title: Logic-Based Explainability in Machine Learning
authors: Joao Marques-Silva
venue: Reasoning Web 2022 lecture notes (per Semantic Scholar); arXiv 2211.00541
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: propositional and first-order logic (prime implicants, abduction, minimal hitting sets)
formal_object: Abductive explanation (AXp): a subset-minimal feature set whose fixed values logically entail the prediction. Its dual is the contrastive explanation (CXp); AXps and CXps are minimal hitting sets of each other.
key_formula: \mathrm{WeakAXp}(\mathcal{X}) := \forall(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{F}).\ \bigwedge_{i\in\mathcal{X}}(x_i=v_i)\rightarrow(\kappa(\mathbf{x})=c)
assumptions: Exact logical encoding of the classifier kappa; discrete or encodable features; full model access; computing explanations is intractable for large networks.
relevance: Gives the rigorous notion of a correct (sound) explanation as entailment, and states non-formal explanations' failure as consistency with different predictions. The sufficient/contrastive duality parallels Halpern-Pearl sufficiency and counterfactual causes; usable on an abstracted causal model of the reasoning.

title: Towards a Theory of Faithfulness: Faithful Explanations of Differentiable Classifiers over Continuous Data
authors: Nico Potyka, Xiang Yin, Francesca Toni
formalism: real analysis (local monotonicity, characterization theorems)
