formal_object: Qualitative faithfulness: an attribution's sign matches the local direction of the feature's effect. Quantitative faithfulness: magnitudes are proportional to output change. Theorem: every qualitatively faithful method is qualitatively equivalent to gradient scores.
key_formula: s_{C,l}(\mathbf{x})_i>0 \Rightarrow \big(x>x_i \Rightarrow C_l(\mathbf{x})<C_l(\mathbf{x}_{-i},x)\big)\wedge\big(x<x_i \Rightarrow C_l(\mathbf{x})>C_l(\mathbf{x}_{-i},x)\big)\ \text{for all } |x-x_i|<\epsilon
assumptions: Continuous inputs, differentiable classifier, feature-attribution explanations; local vs global variants.
relevance: One of the few papers that defines faithfulness itself (not a metric) and proves which explanations can satisfy it. A template for stating local versus global faithfulness and proving characterization results.

title: Does It Make Sense to Speak of Introspection in Large Language Models?
authors: Iulia M. Comsa, Murray Shanahan
formalism: semi-formal causal definition
formal_object: Lightweight introspection: an LLM self-report is introspective if it accurately describes an internal state or mechanism of the LLM through a causal process linking that state and the report.
assumptions: A ground-truth internal state or mechanism and a notion of causal linkage; no privileged-access or internality requirement.
relevance: Minimal causal definition (accuracy plus causal connection) that Lindsey and Song et al. build on and criticize. Reads directly as 'the state is an actual cause of a true report', a ready starting point for a Halpern-Pearl formalization.

title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
authors: Mukund Sundararajan, Ankur Taly, Qiqi Yan
formalism: axiomatic (cooperative game theory / path methods)
formal_object: Axioms an attribution method should satisfy: Sensitivity, Implementation Invariance and Completeness (attributions sum to the output difference from a baseline). Integrated Gradients satisfies them.
key_formula: \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{IntegratedGrads}_i(x)=F(x)-F(x')
assumptions: Differentiable model, a baseline input x', feature-level attributions.
relevance: Canonical axiomatic approach. Implementation Invariance makes attributions a function of input-output behaviour alone, so axioms of this kind cannot capture process faithfulness of CoT. Its 'completeness' differs from a CoT disclosing all causal factors.

title: On the (In)fidelity and Sensitivity for Explanations
authors: Chih-Kuan Yeh, Cheng-Yu Hsieh, Arun Sai Suggala, David I. Inouye, Pradeep Ravikumar
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: probability (expected squared error under a perturbation distribution)
formal_object: Explanation infidelity: expected squared gap between the output change predicted by the explanation and the actual change under perturbations I drawn from mu_I. Includes optimal explanations and the companion max-sensitivity.
key_formula: \mathrm{INFD}(\Phi,f,x)=\mathbb{E}_{I\sim\mu_I}\Big[\big(I^\top\Phi(f,x)-(f(x)-f(x-I))\big)^2\Big]
assumptions: Real-valued model output; a chosen distribution of 'meaningful' perturbations; linear explanation functional.
relevance: Presented as the definition of (in)fidelity. Makes explicit that faithfulness is relative to a chosen intervention distribution, a parameter any causal definition of CoT faithfulness must also fix.

title: Axiomatic Foundations of Explainability
authors: Leila Amgoud, Jonathan Ben-Naim
formalism: axiomatic, logic
formal_object: Axioms for global class explainers (Success, Irreducibility, Feasibility, Coherence, Coreness, Exhaustivity, Completeness...). Coreness and Exhaustivity are incompatible, which separates sufficient-reason from necessary-reason explainers. Anchors/LIME abstractions violate the axiom that prevents incorrect explanations.
key_formula: \forall L\in F(Q),\ \forall I\in \mathrm{Inst}_T \text{ s.t. } L\subseteq I,\ I\in \mathrm{Inst}_T^{R}(x)
assumptions: Finite feature theory, classifier as a function over instances, explanations as sets of literals.
relevance: Axiomatic, impossibility-bearing account of what an explanation must satisfy. Its split between sufficient and necessary reasons corresponds to the soundness and completeness directions a faithful CoT must have.

title: Which Explanation Should I Choose? A Function Approximation Perspective to Characterizing Post Hoc Explanations
authors: Tessa Han, Suraj Srinivas, Himabindu Lakkaraju
formalism: learning theory (local function approximation)
formal_object: Eight attribution methods unified as local function approximation, differing only in neighbourhood and loss. Faithfulness is approximation quality over the neighbourhood. No-free-lunch theorem: no method is optimal across all neighbourhoods.
assumptions: Explanations are local surrogate models; a neighbourhood distribution and a loss are specified.
relevance: A unifying framework plus an impossibility result: faithfulness is indexed by the neighbourhood (set of counterfactual inputs). A CoT definition must also say over which interventions it is faithful.

title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
authors: Fazl Barez, Tung-Yu Wu, Ivan Arcuschin, Michael Lan, Vincent Wang, Noah Siegel, Nicolas Collignon, Clement Neo, Isabelle Lee, Alasdair Paren, Adel Bibi, Robert Trager, Damiano Fornasiere, John Yan, Yanai Elazar, Yoshua Bengio
formalism: semi-formal (verbal jointly necessary conditions)
formal_object: A CoT is faithful if it is procedurally sound, causally relevant (negating a step must change the answer, else the step is irrelevant) and complete (discloses all relevant causal aspects), i.e. correct and reflecting the decision process.
assumptions: A normative standard of correct reasoning; ability to intervene on CoT steps (negation); a notion of the model's 'relevant causal aspects'.
relevance: The most explicit concept-level specification of CoT faithfulness among the seeds. Its three conditions (soundness, necessity under negation, completeness) are the natural targets for a Halpern-Pearl formalization; semi-formal only.

title: When Are Concept Bottleneck Model Explanations Faithful and Compact?
authors: Stefano Teso, Emanuele Marconato, Steve Azzolin, Antonio Vergari
formalism: formal (logic-based) explainability over concept variables
formal_object: Faithful concept-bottleneck explanation: one that does not misreport which concepts actually matter, in the formal-explainability sense. Theorem: for widespread CBM architectures, faithful explanations must include all bottleneck concepts.
assumptions: Model factorizes through a concept bottleneck; concepts as logits or random variables; formal (sufficient-reason) explanations.
relevance: A CoT can be read as a textual bottleneck between input and answer. This impossibility-style result says when compact faithful explanations of bottleneck models exist, and bears on whether a CoT can be both short and complete.

title: Attribution-based Explanations that Provide Recourse Cannot be Robust
authors: Hidde Fokkema, Rianne de Heide, Tim van Erven
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research (per Semantic Scholar); arXiv 2205.15834
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: real analysis (formal impossibility theorem)
formal_object: Recourse sensitivity, defined via a user utility function, for local attributions and counterfactual explanations. Theorem: no single attribution method can be both recourse-sensitive and robust in general.
assumptions: Local attribution or counterfactual explanations; a utility over decision changes; continuity/robustness notion on inputs.
relevance: Impossibility result showing that counterfactual informativeness and stability of explanations trade off. Warns that a definition demanding both counterfactual faithfulness and robustness of rationales may be unsatisfiable.

title: Typed Chain-of-Thought: A Curry-Howard Framework for Verifying LLM Reasoning
authors: Elija Perrier
formalism: type theory (Curry-Howard correspondence)
formal_object: A faithful reasoning trace is analogous to a well-typed program: each CoT step maps to a typed inference, and a successful mapping is a certificate of 'computational faithfulness'.
assumptions: CoT steps can be extracted and mapped to a typed proof structure; a type system for the domain.
relevance: One of the few formal criteria stated directly for CoT. It formalizes procedural soundness and checkability, not causal faithfulness to the model's computation, which shows that the two are distinct.

title: Direct and Indirect Effects
authors: Judea Pearl
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural causal models; nested counterfactuals (natural direct and indirect effects)
formal_object: Natural direct effect: the change in Y when X moves from x* to x while mediator Z keeps the value it would take under x*. The natural indirect effect is the converse; both generalize to path-specific effects.
key_formula: NDE(x,x^*;Y)=E\big(Y_{x,Z_{x^*}}\big)-E\big(Y_{x^*}\big),\qquad NIE(x,x^*;Y)=E\big(Y_{x^*,Z_{x}}\big)-E\big(Y_{x^*}\big)
assumptions: An SCM with the CoT as mediator Z between an input feature X and the answer Y. Cross-world counterfactuals. Average effects identified under Pearl's no-confounding conditions; CoT editing gives experimental access to Z.
relevance: Template for 'the input affects the answer only through the stated reasoning': faithful iff NDE is about 0, post-hoc iff NIE through the CoT is about 0. Four map papers cite it and CASE uses it; no search covered it.

title: Identifiability of Path-Specific Effects
authors: Chen Avin, Ilya Shpitser, Judea Pearl
venue: IJCAI 2005 (full version: UCLA technical report R-321-L)
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural causal models; path-specific counterfactuals; graphical identification
formal_object: Path-specific effect: the effect of one variable on another along a chosen set of causal paths, specified by fixing the parent of each excluded edge at its reference value. Graphical conditions give experimental identifiability.
assumptions: A known causal graph containing the chosen paths. Controlled experiments on the variables involved.
relevance: When the input reaches the answer both through the CoT and through a direct internal route, the effect 'through the stated reasoning' is path-specific. These conditions say when CoT-editing experiments identify it.

title: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness
authors: Silvia Chiappa, Thomas P. S. Gillam
concepts: counterfactuals as used to test explanations
formalism: structural causal models; path-specific counterfactuals
formal_object: A decision system is fair when it disregards the effect of a sensitive attribute along designated unfair causal pathways while keeping its effect along fair pathways.
assumptions: A known causal graph with pathways labelled fair or unfair. A latent-variable model to compute corrected counterfactual observations.
relevance: A worked template for defining a property of a predictor as counterfactual invariance along specified paths. Replacing 'unfair paths' with 'paths that bypass the CoT' yields a path-specific definition of CoT faithfulness.

title: Security Policies and Security Models
authors: J. A. Goguen, J. Meseguer
venue: 1982 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (doi:10.1109/SP.1982.10014)
formalism: state machines; information-flow security (noninterference, including intransitive policies)
formal_object: Noninterference: a group G does not interfere with group G' if deleting every command issued by G leaves all outputs seen by members of G' unchanged. Security policies are sets of such assertions, and intransitive flows are allowed.
key_formula: G :| G' \iff \forall w\in(U\times C)^*,\ \forall u\in G':\ [\![w]\!]_u=[\![p_G(w)]\!]_u
assumptions: A deterministic state-machine model, a split into sources and observers, and the purge function p_G deleting G's commands.
relevance: The canonical formal notion of 'no hidden channel'. Steganography violates noninterference toward a receiver but not toward the monitor. Intransitive policies express 'information may reach the answer only through the CoT'.

title: Measuring information leakage using generalized gain functions
authors: Mário S. Alvim, Kostas Chatzikokolakis, Catuscia Palamidessi, Geoffrey Smith
venue: IEEE 25th Computer Security Foundations Symposium (CSF 2012), pp. 265-279
formalism: quantitative information flow; probabilistic channels; gain functions (g-leakage)
formal_object: g-leakage: how much observing a channel's output raises an adversary's expected gain from guessing a secret. A gain function scores guesses, so partial, approximate or property-level guesses count. Bounds relate g-capacity to min- and Shannon capacity.
assumptions: A prior over secrets, a probabilistic channel from secret to observation, and an adversary-specific gain function.
relevance: Monitorability as leakage of a hidden attribute (intent, misbehavior) through the CoT to a monitor whose task is the gain function. Its leakage ordering compares CoTs across all monitors. Complements V-information.

title: Bayesian Persuasion
authors: Emir Kamenica, Matthew Gentzkow
formalism: game theory / information design (sender commits to a signal; Bayesian receiver)
formal_object: A sender chooses a signal, an information structure, to influence a Bayesian receiver's action. The paper gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a signal to benefit the sender and characterizes sender-optimal signals.
assumptions: Common prior, a Bayesian receiver, sender commitment to the signal, known payoffs.
relevance: Formalizes misleading without lying: a CoT can contain only true statements yet be chosen to move a monitor's belief. This separates honesty (truthful content) from faithfulness and obfuscation (what is disclosed).

title: Incentivizing honest performative predictions with proper scoring rules
authors: Caspar Oesterheld, Johannes Treutlein, Emery Cooper, Rubi Hudson
formalism: decision theory; proper scoring rules; fixed points
formal_object: A performative prediction is honest (a fixed point) if it accurately reflects the expert's beliefs after the prediction is made. Score-maximizing reports generally are not fixed points; bounds and possibility results follow.
assumptions: Outcomes that depend on the report through a bounded influence. An expert with beliefs who maximizes expected score.
relevance: CoTs and self-reports condition the model's later tokens, so they are performative. This defines honesty for reports that change what they describe, and shows proper scoring, the usual reward form, does not secure it.

title: The Logic of Explanatory Power
authors: Jonah N. Schupbach, Jan Sprenger
formalism: Bayesian probability; axiomatic (conditions of adequacy CA1-CA7)
formal_object: Explanatory power of an explanans h over an explanandum e: the unique measure, valued in [-1, 1], that satisfies seven adequacy conditions, computed from the evaluating agent's probabilities.
key_formula: \mathcal{E}(e,h)=\frac{\Pr(h\mid e)-\Pr(h\mid\neg e)}{\Pr(h\mid e)+\Pr(h\mid\neg e)}
assumptions: A probability function of the evaluating agent over explanans and explanandum. No causal model.
relevance: Plausibility has no formal definition. This measures how well an explanation accounts for the outcome by the reader's lights. Paired with a causal faithfulness condition, it isolates plausible but unfaithful rationalizations.

title: A Formal Account of Dishonesty
authors: Chiaki Sakama, Martin Caminada, Andreas Herzig
venue: Logic Journal of the IGPL 23(2): 259-294 (extends JELIA 2010)
formalism: propositional multi-modal logic of belief, intention and communication
formal_object: Two definitions of lying, lying with objectives, bullshit, withholding information and half-truths, with their logical properties and their relation to deception.
assumptions: Belief and intention modalities for speaker and hearer. Explicit communicative acts.
relevance: The only formal account found of withholding information and half-truths, the dishonesty types closest to an incomplete or selectively verbalized CoT. Complements van Ditmarsch (lying) and Ward (causal deception).

title: Defeat Devices in AI Systems
authors: Emilio Ferrara
formalism: probabilistic behavioral definition over evaluation and deployment input distributions
formal_object: A model has a defeat device if some input property discriminates evaluation from deployment inputs, the output distribution changes with it in a concealed (undeclared) way, and the stated criterion scores higher in evaluation than in deployment.
key_formula: (i)\ P_{eval}(\pi)\neq P_{deploy}(\pi);\ (ii)\ M(\cdot\mid\pi=1)\neq M(\cdot\mid\pi=0),\ \pi\ \text{not declared};\ (iii)\ E_{eval}[\varphi_{stated}(M)]-E_{deploy}[\varphi_{stated}(M)]\geq\Delta>0
assumptions: Evaluation and deployment input distributions, a stated pass criterion, black-box access to input-output behavior. No intent condition, by design.
relevance: The only definition found that covers sandbagging, alignment faking and evaluation-gated scheming at once. Its concealment clause excludes swaps declared in the CoT, which connects scheming to faithfulness. Behavioral, not causal.

title: A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings
authors: Brian Maniscalco, Hakwan Lau
formalism: signal detection theory (type-2 sensitivity, meta-d')
formal_object: meta-d': metacognitive (type-2) sensitivity, i.e. how well confidence reports discriminate one's own correct from incorrect decisions, in signal-to-noise units, free of response bias and type-1 sensitivity.
assumptions: Binary type-1 decisions with graded confidence ratings. An SDT model of the type-1 task.
relevance: Cognitive science's standard formal criterion for metacognitive accuracy. It separates report accuracy from task accuracy, which LLM introspection tests conflate, but it is measurement-level and needs adaptation for open-ended answers.

title: Model Interpretability through the Lens of Computational Complexity
authors: Pablo Barceló, Mikaël Monet, Jorge Pérez, Bernardo Subercaseaux
formalism: computational complexity of explanation queries
formal_object: A model class C1 is more interpretable than C2 if answering local post-hoc explanation queries, such as minimal sufficient reasons, is computationally harder for C2 than for C1.
assumptions: Fixed explanation queries, standard complexity assumptions (P != NP), comparisons between model classes rather than individual models.
relevance: An observer-free formal reading of simulatability as tractability of explanation queries. It pairs with resource-bounded observer definitions (V-information, Song et al.) for the legibility of reasoning.

title: The Compliance Gap: Why AI Systems Promise to Follow Process Instructions but Don't
authors: Kwan Soo Shin
formalism: information theory (data processing inequality); RL incentive argument
formal_object: Compliance gap: a verbal commitment to a process that the executed behavior does not follow. Theorem 1 says RL that rewards text without observing behavior makes it inevitable. Theorem 2 says no observer can detect it from text alone.
assumptions: Observers see text only, without tool-call logs. Training rewards text without observing behavior.
relevance: A say-do notion of honesty with a text-only undetectability theorem, the agentic analogue of CoT unfaithfulness. Theorems not checked in the full text; the undetectability result looks close to definitional.
